title: Australia to export AI compute as data centre demand surges
full_text:
The vast majority of processing in the data centres being rolled out around the country will be for American technology giants, forcing cloud computing and digital infrastructure developers to defend the construction of the assets as something that will benefit local communities.
That’s the view of Boris Dangubic, the head of business development for Iren, a Sydney-headquartered, Nasdaq-listed cloud computing operator that has proposed a $10 billion project in the tiny South Australian town of Bundey and now has a market capitalisation of almost $25 billion.
Iren’s Boris Dangubic at the summit on Monday. Dominic Lorrimer
“Based on the outlook in terms of the number of data centres that are being built and the sheer quantum of tokens [units of data] that will be generated here, the vast majority would be going offshore, and will effectively be exporting intelligence,” Dangubic told The Australian Financial Review Property Summit, adding that the country had the renewable energy capacity and engineering capabilities to build “a real export business in the same way that we’ve done in mining”.
While backlash against data centres has become mainstream in the United States, particularly amid concerns about massive power and water use, local community opposition to big projects has only just started to grow.
In a submission to a senate inquiry into the sector, for instance, Sydney University researchers said that without deliberate government intervention, “Australia risks becoming a mere ‘resource provider’ for the global digital economy – supplying the land, energy, and water – while the vast economic value and governance benefits are extracted offshore”.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who has described artificial intelligence as the “the biggest economic transformation in our lifetime”, wants hyperscalers such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Meta and Google as well as AI model providers such as Open AI and Anthropic to process data locally.
Dangubic said local communities would benefit from the “significant” local taxes Iren would pay and from the creation of jobs at those projects. Iren has said it has signed up a “leading frontier lab” as one of its global customers, but declined to confirm speculation that this was Anthropic.
Demand for data centres is soaring.
Macquarie Data Centres chief executive David Hirst said the company could not build infrastructure fast enough, adding “speed gets you deals”.
Land accounted for about 10 per cent of a data centre’s costs, with mechanical and electrical equipment accounting for about 70 per cent, Hirst said, while the computing equipment that goes inside the building cost about five times as much as the entire data centre. “If you’ve got a circa $3 billion site, you’ve got $15 billion worth of computer equipment inside the site,” he said.
Victoria Hardie, group operating officer for HMC Capital, which owns just over 20 per cent of ASX-listed data centre operator DigiCo Infrastructure, warned that developing new sites was becoming “increasingly difficult” despite the demand for capacity. “The social licence aspect has really ramped up significantly in the last three months,” she said.
Multiplex’s general counsel Meg Redwin said most data centres built by the construction group, which is being acquired by Japan’s Obayashi Corporation, were “modularised” so that they could be delivered quickly.
“They’re big packages,” Redwin said, adding that mechanical and electrical subcontracts could be worth $160 million alone. “You can build a lot of [residential] or commercial for that sort of money.”
Equinix’s Asia Pacific senior director for real estate, Tim Robinson, said zoning land for data centres, including specifying sites for projects with a particular power capacity, would help developers. The US company, which operates about 40 data centres locally, is focused on building around its existing sites in industrial areas but expects to have to move new developments into regional areas due to competition for land.
